x.ASV: For the Chief Musician. A Psalm of David. The king shall joy in thy strength, O Jehovah; And in thy salvation how greatly shall he rejoice!
x.Darby: To the chief Musician. A Psalm of David. The king shall joy in thy strength, Jehovah; and in thy salvation how greatly shall he rejoice.
x.KJV: To the chief Musician, A Psalm of David. The king shall joy in thy strength, O Lord; and in thy salvation how greatly shall he rejoice!
x.YLT: To the Overseer. --A Psalm of David. Jehovah, in Thy strength is the king joyful, In Thy salvation how greatly he rejoiceth.

nt: If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **strength** and **salvation**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [because you are strong … and because you save me] or [because you are powerful … and because you save those who trust in you]

You may be used to indicating when David is referring to himself in the third person by saying something such as “I, the king rejoice … I exult.” However, we recommend that you not do that in this instance, since **the king** here, while including David, refers to others besides him.

David is using a phrase that expresses a strong feeling of joy. There may be an equivalent word or phrase in your language that you can use in your translation to convey this feeling. Alternate translation: [he rejoices so very much] or [he is extremely glad]

x.ASV: Thou hast given him his heart’s desire, And hast not withholden the request of his lips. [Selah
x.Darby: Thou hast given him his heart's desire, and hast not withholden the request of his lips. Selah.
x.KJV: Thou hast given him his heart’s desire, and hast not withholden the request of his lips. Selah.
x.YLT: The desire of his heart Thou gavest to him, And the request of his lips Thou hast not withheld. Selah.

nt: If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **desire**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [what he desired]

Here the **heart** represents where a person’s desires exist. You may have a comparable expression in your language, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [what he desired] or [what he desired in his inmost being]

Here, **the request of his lips** represents what the king asked for by using his lips to speak. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and what he asked for]

x.ASV: For thou meetest him with the blessings of goodness: Thou settest a crown of fine gold on his head.
x.Darby: For thou hast met him with the blessings of goodness; thou hast set a crown of pure gold on his head.
x.KJV: For thou preventest him with the blessings of goodness: thou settest a crown of pure gold on his head.
x.YLT: For Thou puttest before him blessings of goodness, Thou settest on his head a crown of fine gold.

nt: Here the phrase **you meet him** could mean: (1) that Yahweh met the king. Alternate translation: [you come to him with good blessings] or [you greet him with excellent blessings], or (2) that Yahweh anticipated what the king needed and was already working ahead of time before the king prayed in order to meet his needs. Alternate translation: [you anticipated his needs and came to him with blessings of good] or [you knew what he needed and met him with blessings of good]

The implication is that God blesses the king with good things. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [with good blessings] or [with excellent blessings]
This is poetic language. If your language has a way to indicate poetry, you could use it here. Alternate translation: [with rich blessings]

David assumes that readers will know that Yahweh himself did not physically **place** a crown on David’s head but rather chose him to be king and had people crown him as king by placing a crown on his head. You could say that explicitly if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [you cause to be placed]

Placing **a crown** on the king’s **head** was a symbolic action by which God showed that he was establishing the king in his royal authority and giving him honor. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the significance of this action in the text of your translation or in a footnote. Alternate translation: [you place on his head a crown of refined gold, showing that you have established him as king]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **life**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [He asked you that he might live, and you granted his request and gave him length of days, forever and ever]

David assumes that readers will know that **length of days** means to live for many years. You could say that explicitly if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [a long life] or [a lengthy life]

If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **salvation**, **splendor**, and **majesty**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [You glorify him greatly by saving him; you make him splendorous and majestic]

The terms **splendor** and **majesty** mean similar things. David is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [great honor you place on him] or [magnificent glory you place on him]

David assumes that readers will know that **place on him** here means “give to him.” You could say that explicitly if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [you bestow on him] or [you give to him]

x.Darby: For thou hast made him to be blessings for ever; thou hast filled him with joy by thy countenance.
x.KJV: For thou hast made him most blessed for ever: thou hast made him exceeding glad with thy countenance.
x.YLT: For Thou makest him blessings for ever, Thou dost cause him to rejoice with joy, By Thy countenance.

nt: David assumes that readers will know that **him** refers to the king mentioned in the superscription and throughout the psalm. You could say that explicitly if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [you bestow on the king] or [you grant the king]
תְשִׁיתֵ֣⁠הוּ בְרָכ֣וֹת לָ⁠עַ֑ד תְּחַדֵּ֥⁠הוּ בְ֝⁠שִׂמְחָ֗ה אֶת־פָּנֶֽי⁠ךָ

The implication is that the king will rejoice in the presence of God, that is, he will rejoice because God is with him. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [you make him glad with joy because you are present with him] or [you make him rejoice because he is in your presence]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **blessings**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [you bless him eternally]
This is poetic language. If your language has a way to indicate poetry, you could use it here. Alternate translation: [you make him very glad] or [you make him exceedingly glad]

Here, **with your face** represents being in Yahweh’s presence. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [in your presence] or [with your presence]

x.ASV: Thy hand will find out all thine enemies; Thy right hand will find out those that hate thee.
x.Darby: Thy hand shall find out all thine enemies; thy right hand shall find out those that hate thee.
x.KJV: Thine hand shall find out all thine enemies: thy right hand shall find out those that hate thee.
x.YLT: Thy hand cometh to all Thine enemies, Thy right hand doth find Thy haters.

nt: תִּמְצָ֣א יָ֭דְ⁠ךָ לְ⁠כָל־אֹיְבֶ֑י⁠ךָ יְ֝מִֽינְ⁠ךָ תִּמְצָ֥א שֹׂנְאֶֽי⁠ךָ

These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and you may want to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation. If it is helpful, you could connect the phrases in a way that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: [Your hand will find all of your enemies, indeed, your right hand will find those who hate you]
The pronoun **Your** refers to the king. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [You, the king’s hand] or [The king’s hand]

David is using **Your hand will find** as a common expression of his culture to mean “You will reach” or “You will overtake.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [You will reach … you will overtake]

x.ASV: Thou wilt make them as a fiery furnace in the time of thine anger: Jehovah will swallow them up in his wrath, And the fire shall devour them.
x.Darby: Thou shalt make them as a fiery furnace in the time of thy presence; Jehovah shall swallow them up in his anger, and the fire shall devour them:
x.KJV: Thou shalt make them as a fiery oven in the time of thine anger: the Lord shall swallow them up in his wrath, and the fire shall devour them.
x.YLT: Thou makest them as a furnace of fire, At the time of Thy presence. Jehovah in His anger doth swallow them, And fire doth devour them.

nt: The pronoun **them** refers to the king’s enemies. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [You, the king, will make your enemies]

The point of this comparison is that just as **an oven of fire** completely consumes what is placed in it, so David is saying that God will completely destroy his enemies. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [You will completely consume them like fire in an oven]

David is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [You will make them as something that is burned in an oven of fire]
Here, **your face** represents your presence. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [at the time of your appearing]

David is using the phrase **In his nose** as a common expression of the culture to mean that Yahweh is angry. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [In his anger] or [In his wrath]

David is speaking of Yahweh destroying his enemies as if Yahweh will literally **swallow** them and burn them up with **fire**. If these images communicate well in your language, please use them. If not, you could express the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Yahweh will destroy them completely, as if swallowing them or consuming them with fire]

These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and you may want to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation. If it is helpful, you could connect the phrases in a way that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: [Yahweh will completely destroy them as if he was swallowing them; yes, he will consume them as if he was burning them with fire]

x.ASV: Their fruit wilt thou destroy from the earth, And their seed from among the children of men.
x.Darby: Their fruit shalt thou destroy from the earth, and their seed from among the children of men.
x.KJV: Their fruit shalt thou destroy from the earth, and their seed from among the children of men.
x.YLT: Their fruit from earth Thou destroyest, And their seed from the sons of men.

nt: The pronoun **You** refers to the king. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [You, God’s king, will destroy]

David is speaking of **their fruit** and **their seed** as if his enemies’ descendants were literal **fruit** and literal **seed** that could be destroyed. If this image does not communicate well in your language, you could express this as a comparison or use plain language. Alternate translation: [their descendants … and their offspring]

David is using **from among the sons of man** as a common expression of his culture to mean “from among humanity” or “from the human race.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [from among the human race] or [from among humanity]

Here David is speaking of the king’s enemies’ plans to harm him as if they would physically **stretch out evil** like a net or trap. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a comparable expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [they plan to harm you] or [they devise evil schemes against you]

David is using the adjective **evil** as a noun to mean a certain kind of thing. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [they stretch out evil things against you]

David is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [they plan a plot they will not be able to accomplish]

x.Darby: Be thou exalted, Jehovah, in thine own strength: we will sing and celebrate thy power.
x.KJV: Be thou exalted, Lord, in thine own strength: so will we sing and praise thy power.

nt: If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **strength** and **power**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [Be exalted, Yahweh, because you are strong … and we will praise you because of how powerful you are]

The implication is that this singing and praising will happen after Yahweh shows his strength by defeating the enemies. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [then we will sing and we will praise your power]
